Cats. Cats is a 1981 musical by composer Andrew Lloyd Webber, based on T.S. Eliot's poetry collection Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats. It revolutionized musical theatre by abandoning traditional narrative, instead presenting a kaleidoscopic parade of feline characters. The show is structured as a nighttime ball where various cats introduce themselves through stylized dance and song, prioritizing spectacle and character vignettes over story. Webber adapted his melodies from Eliot's witty and whimsical 1939 poetry collection.

One song in particular broke through to mainstream success. "Memory" became a concert standard and one of the most-recorded musical theatre songs, sung by Grizabella the Glamour Cat as she recalls her faded past.

The cast is an eclectic collection of oddball felines. There's Rum Tum Tugger, a pampered narcissist; Mungojerrie and Rumpleteazer, a pair of cat burglars; and Old Deuteronomy, a patriarchal elder who presides over the ball.

The show opened on Broadway in 1982 and ran for eighteen years, delivering seven thousand four hundred eighty-five performances. It won seven Tony Awards including Best Musical in 1983. Though its book is notoriously surreal, audiences embraced it as a unique theatrical experience. The show's durability became even more apparent in 2019, when a film adaptation was widely derided as grotesque, yet sparked renewed cultural conversation about Cats' unusual aesthetic and its seemingly permanent place in audience affection.
